newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Revived Australia dlr elbows aside resistance.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Revived Australia dlr elbows aside resistance.

text.p: The Australian dollar reinforced its rally with another 1/4 cent of gains Wednesday as supporters elbowed aside resistance at US$0.7960 to snatch their third chart scalp of the week.

The forces behind the push were much the same that had rescued it from a US$0.7815 trough a fortnight ago. Japanese hunger for the A$'s high yield was reflected in fresh samurai buying and U.S. and European investors were no less keen.
Firmer commodity prices provided a positive sub-text while the seizure of a string of important technical levels excited chart watchers who were tipping a test of 80 cents near term.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) an increasingly confident currency had barged its way to US$0.7962/67, its best finish in a month, from an early US$0.7944/49 and US$0.7940/45 late here on Tuesday.
The latest push brought its gains for the week to 2/3 cent and its tally of captured chart barriers to three; US$0.7920, US$0.7940 and US$0.7960.

All of which came as a suprise to most dealers who had been square -- in more ways than one -- after weeks of aimless range trading. "It's been a rally by stealth," said one. "The buying has been sizeable and widespread, but what made it effective was that nobody was looking for a sustained rise."

Traders felt the rally could still fizzle out, as so many others have, in the face of major chart resistance in the US$0.8000/8020 area and would not be inclined to go long until that barrier were cleared.
Technical analysts were more upbeat given the close atop US$0.7960 and looked for a test there soon with a break promising to ignite a new multi-month uptrend to 84 cents.

Dealers attributed much of the improvement to the continued inflow of Japanese funds from investors desperate to escape record low rates at home. This had assured a steady flow of yen/A$ samurai bonds, another of which was launched today.

This demand had so far survived a score of scares over possible Japanese tightenings, but bulls did feel intimations of mortality recently as the authorities there began to turn upbeat on prospects for the economy.

Japanese government officials caused a stir today by telling Reuters that recent rises in yen bond prices were clearly at odds with the performance of the economy, in which production had begun to show some strength.
The comment drove Japanese bond yields higher and pushed the yen up across the board as the market wondered if it was not being softened up for a rate hike down the road.

Analysts were more sanguine in the belief the MOF was really trying to puncture a potentially damaging speculative bubble that had been forming in the JGB market and had no intention of raising rates while the banking system was so fragile.
The position of the Bank of Japan on all this might become a little clearer when governor Yasuo Matsushita holds a press conference this evening.

Bulls will be hoping he repeats the standard formula that policy needs to be kept easy to support Japan's economic recovery. Any fudging on this issue could reinforce the impression a tightening was in the wind and hurt both dollars.
That caution kept the local dollar in check at 88.54/64 yen today, having jumped nearly a yen to 88.67/77 on Tuesday. In trade weighted terms it inched up to 58.5 from 58.4.
The only domestic data out was the Westpac leading index for September which eased 0.4 point or 0.3 percent.

Elsewhere, commodity prices were mixed but with pockets of strength, notably copper which shot to five-month highs Tuesday. The Commodity Research Bureau futures index continued its recent bounce rising 1.04 points to 245.51, putting it comfortably above the November 5 trough of 235.99 but still far below the April peak of 263.79. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
